strengths: Novel theoretical framework: Theorem 3.4 provides an interesting unified analysis showing all normalized attention mechanisms disperse (assign near-equal weights) as n→∞, encompassing softmax, linear, and other variants within a single generalized framework.

Principled design motivation: Rather than ad-hoc fixes, the paper uses the proved dispersion property to justify a simple averaging mechanism for global information aggregation, grounded in theoretical analysis.
Comprehensive attention analysis: The generalized attention definition (Definition 3.3) successfully unifies multiple attention variants and clearly characterizes their dispersion bounds in Table 1.

Consistent experimental improvements: Demonstrates 0.2% gains on ImageNet-1K (83.7% vs MILA-T 83.5%) and 0.5-0.7% improvements at larger image resolutions (384², 672², 768²), with competitive COCO results.
Simple and practical design: SEMA elegantly combines window attention with uniform averaging in a straightforward mechanism with minimal computational overhead.
weaknesses: Critical theory-practice gap: Theorem 3.4 addresses asymptotic behavior (n→∞), but practical images have finite tokens (~50K for 224²). Dispersion bounds Θ(1/n) are loose at practical scales, and the paper provides no empirical validation that attention actually disperses on real vision tasks.

Severely limited experimental scope: Experiments restricted to tiny (~30M parameter) models only. Generalization to base/large models is entirely unknown. This substantially reduces impact and applicability to modern vision research.

Modest and potentially non-significant improvements: +0.2% on ImageNet-1K and comparable performance on COCO lack error bars and multiple runs. Given small magnitude, improvements may be within noise margins.

Insufficient efficiency validation: Despite 'Scalable and Efficient' in title, no runtime, memory, or throughput measurements provided. FLOPs are actually higher for SEMA at larger resolutions (40G vs 43G at 672²), contradicting efficiency claims.

Design choices inadequately justified: Uniform 1/n averaging for global information lacks theoretical or empirical justification. Why not learned or attention-weighted averaging? No ablation on window size, positional encoding interactions, or averaging strategies beyond uniform.

Restrictive theoretical assumptions: Compactness assumption (Remark 3.5) is problematic for deep networks where features after multiple nonlinear transformations may not remain bounded. The provided counterexample shows theorem can fail, weakening practical applicability.
Limited downstream task evaluation: Only COCO evaluated; generalization to video, 3D, or other domains unknown. Narrow experimental domain limits significance assessment.

Missing empirical dispersion validation: No visualization or measurement demonstrating attention actually disperses in practice or that averaging approximates dispersed behavior, leaving key theoretical claims unvalidated empirically.

strengths: Solid theoretical framework: Theorem 3.3 provides a general, unified formulation of attention dispersion across softmax and linear variants with sound proofs
Novel large-resolution evaluation: Systematic experiments on 384², 672², 768², 1024² show substantial improvements (7.3% at 1024², 33% speedup at 2048²) that are rarely reported
Comprehensive experimental validation: Thorough evaluation across ImageNet-1K, COCO, and ADE20K with detailed ablations and runtime analysis
Probabilistic perspective: Proposition 3.5 provides complementary theoretical understanding of dispersion
Clean and efficient design: Window attention + averaging is simple, interpretable, and computationally efficient
weaknesses: Theory-practice gap: Theorem 3.3 proves n→∞ asymptotics, but standard vision models have moderate tokens (3136 at 224², 49 at stage 4). Authors acknowledge averaging contributes only +0.2% at 224², undermining the theoretical motivation

Limited novelty of core insight: Dispersion phenomenon already identified by Veličković et al. (2025). The general formulation is useful but not groundbreaking. The solution (window + averaging) is straightforward given this observation

Modest standard-resolution improvements: Only +0.4% over MILA-T at 224² (83.7% vs 83.3%), which is the practical deployment setting. Ablations show value projection, not averaging, drives gains at standard resolutions

Reproducibility concerns: Single-run evaluations acknowledged as typical due to resource constraints, but this limits statistical significance. Claims of consistency across runs are stated without supporting evidence (error bars, multiple runs shown). Limited hyperparameter tuning with window size sensitivity

Loose theoretical bounds: Authors acknowledge bounds are not tight. Dispersion coefficients range 10¹-10⁶ empirically, making theoretical bounds uninformative. Causal Mamba doesn't disperse, weakening generality of averaging motivation

Gap between stated contributions and ablations: The averaging term (theoretically motivated) contributes minimally at 224² (+0.2%) and only becomes pronounced at non-standard large resolutions (672²: +2.2%). At typical deployment resolutions, improvements come from value projection—not the theoretical insight
Vision-only evaluation: Despite claims about general attention mechanisms, experiments limited to vision. No NLP tasks to test asymptotic theory where long sequences are common

Confounding factors: Shared KV representation across heads is orthogonal to dispersion problem but could contribute to improvements. Insufficient ablation to isolate the averaging component's true contribution

strengths: Solid theoretical framework generalizing dispersion phenomenon with formal Theorem 3.3, though similar to concurrent work
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across ImageNet-1K (multiple resolutions), COCO, and ADE20K with detailed ablations
Honest discussion of limitations including asymptotic nature of theory, single-run experiments, and scope to vision tasks
Good presentation overall with clear notation and structured development of ideas from theory to practice
Strong performance on large-resolution image scaling (7.3% improvement over VMamba at 1024²), suggesting potential for high-resolution applications
weaknesses: Severe theory-practice gap: dispersion theory motivates averaging component, but ablation (Table 8) shows averaging contributes only +0.2% at 224² (standard resolution), contradicting the motivation
Critical reproducibility issue: marginal improvements (0.2-0.4% on ImageNet) reported from single runs without confidence intervals or multiple seeds—insufficient rigor for ICML

Limited novelty: SEMA is straightforward combination of Swin window attention (2021) + trivial averaging (1/n·Σv) + value projection; core theoretical insight about dispersion is credited to Veličković et al. (2025)
Confounding experimental factors: value projection explains -0.8% loss vs averaging's -0.2% (Table 7), suggesting gains primarily from non-theory-motivated components, not averaging
Overclaimed contribution: improvements at large resolutions diminish significantly after fine-tuning (7.3%→0.4%), and comparisons use different baselines (VMamba vs MILA), making attribution unclear
No adaptive or learned averaging despite uniformly applying (1/n)·Σv; missing direct comparison to Veličković et al. (2025)'s temperature scaling solution to dispersion
Compactness assumption in Theorem 3.3 restricts applicability—multi-layer neural networks may produce unbounded activations
Vision-only scope with acknowledged limitations; claims about general attention mechanisms unsubstantiated
Insufficient justification for why window attention is the right component to prevent dispersion or why window+averaging is theoretically motivated

strengths: Strong theoretical contribution: Theorem 3.3 provides a general framework proving that any generalized attention with continuous normalization disperses as tokens increase to infinity, elegantly unifying softmax and linear attention

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple benchmarks (ImageNet-1K at multiple resolutions, COCO, ADE20K) with particularly thorough testing on large image resolutions (384²-1024²) showing clear improvements over VMamba (7.3% gap at 1024²)
Clear theory-to-practice connection: dispersion analysis directly motivates the local-global attention design, making the method development principled rather than ad-hoc
Practical efficiency gains: 33% speedup over MILA at 1024² resolution demonstrating scalability benefits beyond accuracy improvements
Well-structured presentation: clearly written with accessible theoretical framework, comprehensive proofs in appendix, and honest discussion of limitations and assumptions
Rigorous ablation studies (Tables 7-8) showing differential contributions of components across resolutions, demonstrating when and why SEMA helps
weaknesses: Significant theory-practice gap: Theorem 3.3 requires asymptotic n→∞ but practical token counts (56²-256²) may not approach limit; dispersion coefficients φ(b)/φ(a) range from 10³-10⁶; at standard 224² resolution, averaging contributes only +0.2% (Table 8)

Ablation evidence suggests value projection (not dispersion theory) drives improvements: removing value projection causes -0.8% drop vs only -0.2% from removing averaging at 224² (Table 7), undermining the central theoretical motivation for standard benchmarks
Marginal improvements on standard benchmarks: +0.4% on ImageNet-1K 224² (83.7% vs 83.3%), similar patterns on COCO/ADE20K, with main advantage limited to rarely-used large resolutions

Limited methodological novelty: the actual mechanism (window softmax + simple averaging) is straightforward; window attention is well-established (Swin); no exploration of weighted/learned averaging alternatives despite mentioning them in conclusions

Incomplete experimental analysis: no comparison with other dispersion-fixing methods (Veličković et al. 2025, Ye et al. 2024); no ablation separating value projection from averaging effect (e.g., MILA + value projection); minimal window size exploration

Theoretical limitations: Remark 3.4 notes boundedness assumption is strict and may not hold for unbounded feature spaces; the mechanism for why simple averaging specifically mitigates dispersion better than alternatives is not uniquely justified

Limited scope and reproducibility: vision-only evaluation; no language/multimodal experiments despite Mamba's popularity in LLMs; authors report single-run experiments for most results due to resource constraints; limited hyperparameter tuning

Finetuning effects weakly explained: Table 8 shows finetuning can partially mitigate dispersion effects (+2.2% without tuning drops to +0.4% with tuning at 672²), suggesting other learning mechanisms compensate, weakening the necessity argument for theoretical dispersion handling
